narrative.text: The cover page of the French edition of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative Strategic Plan 2004–2008, issued by WHO and the initiative's partners.

The cataloguing and copyright page of the polio eradication strategic plan 2004–2008 (French edition), with ISBN, subject headings, ordering and permissions information and standard disclaimers. It also notes the typesetting and printing in Switzerland.
The title page of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative Strategic Plan 2004–2008 (French edition).

The table of contents of the polio eradication strategic plan (in French), listing the summary, history, goal, four objectives, general challenges, partners' roles and the post-2008 phase of stopping oral polio vaccination.
A list of acronyms used in the polio eradication strategic plan (in French), such as donor agencies, national and local immunization days and vaccine types.

The summary of the polio eradication strategic plan (in French), stating that by end-2003 polio remained in only six countries, nearly five million children had been spared paralysis and vitamin A distribution had averted 1.25 million child deaths. It notes potential savings above US$ 1 billion a year and outlines the plan's four objectives, starting with interrupting wild poliovirus transmission. Footnotes list the remaining endemic countries and note that the plan replaces the 2001–2005 plan.

Continues the summary (in French), describing the products needed to stop oral polio vaccine (OPV) use, such as laboratory containment guidance, monovalent OPV stockpiles and Sabin-strain inactivated vaccine. It describes the fourth objective, integrating polio eradication resources into other disease control programmes, and refers to the separate estimate of financial needs.

Gives the history of the polio eradication initiative (in French), launched by the World Health Assembly in 1988, and its achievements by the end of 2003. A diagram outlines the plan's timeline to 2009 and beyond, including integration of polio resources and the move to long-term polio vaccination policy.

Continues the history (in French), noting that scaled-up eradication reached over 575 million children with OPV by the late 1990s and that polio has been eliminated from 210 countries and territories. It identifies the last transmission chains in Nigeria, India and Pakistan and presents the plan as the basis for partners' annual planning.

States the goal of the polio eradication initiative (in French): to interrupt poliovirus transmission worldwide, secure the benefits of eradication and use its lessons and infrastructure to strengthen health systems.

Describes the strategic approach to interrupting wild poliovirus transmission (in French), combining routine and supplementary immunization with high-quality surveillance. It explains why OPV3 coverage alone did not stop polio in many developing countries, including lower seroconversion in tropical settings. It sets out supplementary immunization plans and synchronized campaigns across countries and regions.

Describes how the World Health Assembly and the Technical Consultative Group urged more national and local immunization days, house-to-house vaccination and a focus of resources on the last endemic areas (in French). It plans intensified mass vaccination campaigns to break remaining transmission chains. A map shows wild poliovirus cases and importations as of December 2003.

Explains that transmission persisted because many young children were missed during immunization days and routine OPV coverage was often below 25% in key reservoirs (in French). It notes repeated importations of wild poliovirus that paralysed more than 70 children between 1999 and 2003. A table lists planned national and local immunization days for 2004–2008.

Focuses on the key reservoir areas in Nigeria, India and Pakistan and the measures needed to reach over 90% of children in intensified campaigns, such as high-level oversight and detailed mapping (in French). It also covers mop-up responses to importations, to be integrated into WHO and UNICEF emergency arrangements by 2007.

Describes supplementary immunization in polio-free areas most at risk of reinfection, including campaigns for two years after the last case in endemic countries (in French). It lists high-risk polio-free countries and a table of routine OPV3 coverage against the target of 90% national coverage by 2010.

Describes strengthening routine immunization with UNICEF and GAVI to limit spread of imported cases and vaccine-derived polioviruses, including a birth dose of OPV (in French). It gives a table of milestones for interrupting transmission, based on interrupting transmission by early 2005 and the Alliance's coverage target.

Sets out the main challenges to interrupting wild poliovirus transmission by end-2004 (in French), noting evidence in mid-2003 that this could be achieved within a year. It discusses the need for better campaign quality, local political engagement and resources in remaining endemic areas, with a footnote defining the immunity gap.

Continues the challenges (in French), including vaccination teams with at least one woman, better accountability in Pakistan's tribal areas and the serious obstacle of intense transmission in northern Nigeria. It also covers vaccine-derived poliovirus risks and improved surveillance to understand them.
Concludes that circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus events should remain rare despite fewer campaigns, with the Technical Consultative Group to review its recommendations by 2005 (in French).

Describes objective 2, achieving global certification of polio eradication by 2008 (in French), noting that three WHO regions were certified by end-2003. It identifies weaknesses in surveillance and in laboratory containment of wild poliovirus as challenges. It explains the acute flaccid paralysis surveillance standards and refers to the WHO laboratory containment action plan.

Describes biosafety rules for inactivated polio vaccine production after transmission ends and the structure of global, regional and national certification commissions (in French). It analyses the status of certification by region and includes a figure on population in regions by certification status.

Describes the global polio laboratory network and its quality assurance, with 99% of laboratories WHO-accredited in 2002 (in French). It reports progress in laboratory containment, with 148 countries having started or completed inventories by mid-2003, and plans to maintain network resources, citing resolution WHA52.22.
Maps of acute flaccid paralysis surveillance performance indicators for 2003, showing non-polio AFP rates and adequate stool collection rates by country, with map disclaimers in English and French.

Describes future laboratory network activity and data needs ahead of global certification, and priorities for containing wild and vaccine-derived polioviruses under the 2003 global action plan (in French). It also covers WHO support to certification commissions.

A table of indicators and annual milestones for objective 2 (in French), covering certification-standard surveillance, testing in accredited laboratories, containment phases, biosafety for inactivated vaccine production and submission of final certification documents from 2004 to 2008.

Describes objective 3, developing products for stopping OPV use globally (in French), explaining that outbreaks of vaccine-derived poliovirus since 2000 show that continued OPV use could threaten eradication. It states that routine OPV use should stop as soon as possible after certification while surveillance and immunity are high. It introduces the policy areas the Technical Consultative Group said must be addressed.

Lists four policy areas for stopping OPV (routine immunization, detection and notification of circulating poliovirus, vaccine stockpiles and outbreak response, and long-term containment) and summarises the 1998 expert consultation on stopping polio vaccination (in French). A table estimates risks of paralytic polio after global certification.

Describes public consultations, including a 2002 meeting and a 2003 consultation that concluded vaccine-derived polioviruses pose a real risk for as long as OPV is used (in French). It explains why OPV should be stopped soon after certification, as surveillance and coverage tend to decline once regions are certified.

Describes encouraging Sabin-strain inactivated polio vaccine and treating any circulating poliovirus detected after eradication as a public health emergency requiring immediate notification (in French). It also covers aligning AFP reporting with other WHO alert systems and developing a containment plan for the OPV cessation phase.

Continues Objective 3 of the French edition of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative Strategic Plan 2004–2008, on preparing products for stopping oral polio vaccine (OPV), describing how a third edition of the laboratory containment action plan will set biosafety standards for Sabin strains and vaccine production sites. It notes that long-term containment monitoring will be harmonized with arrangements for other high-risk pathogens. A table sets yearly milestones from 2004 to 2008 and indicators, such as monovalent OPV stockpiles, licensing Sabin-based inactivated vaccine, integration with the International Health Regulations and OPV cessation.

Introduces Objective 4, integrating the polio eradication initiative into broader health services, noting its support since the mid-1990s for vitamin A distribution, integrated disease surveillance, routine immunization and GAVI activities. It explains how supplementary immunization campaigns were used to add other interventions, upgrade routine services such as the cold chain and training, and build community demand. It adds that coordination bodies such as interagency committees and technical advisory groups have taken on strengthening routine immunization.

Explains that the polio partnership has invested heavily in staff, infrastructure and institutional arrangements, which should be integrated into national immunization and surveillance systems to support goals such as higher routine coverage and lower measles mortality. Its situation analysis notes that polio technical advisory groups now serve wider immunization work, that national interagency coordinating committees became the channel for GAVI support and a model for the Global Fund, and that polio-funded staff already spend much of their time on other priorities. Footnotes cite the advisory groups and a 2001 WHO survey of polio-funded staff.

Gives examples of integration, such as the acute flaccid paralysis network serving as a base for integrated disease surveillance in the WHO African Region and joint polio and measles surveillance in the Americas, and WHO and UNICEF training of polio-funded staff to support routine immunization. It sets out planned work, beginning with transferring polio-funded human resources and engaging stakeholders. It then describes extending acute flaccid paralysis surveillance to other diseases of public health importance.

Describes two approaches to integrating surveillance: merging acute flaccid paralysis surveillance into routine systems where capacity exists, prioritizing certified polio-free countries, or building it up to cover other vaccine-preventable and epidemic-prone diseases elsewhere. It notes that countries needing long-term surveillance support will be identified by the end of 2004. It also discusses applying polio eradication lessons to other health goals, especially the Millennium Development Goal target on child mortality.

Adds that polio experience in human resources, financing and management should support efforts against measles and the expansion of interventions such as vitamin A, insecticide-treated nets and antiretroviral treatment. A table sets yearly percentage targets from 2004 to 2008 for Objective 4 indicators, such as priority countries implementing integrated plans and full integration of polio operations into measles activities.

Opens the chapter on general challenges facing polio eradication, starting with the need for sustained high-level political commitment in endemic and donor countries, supported by country-by-country advocacy. It then covers external financing, noting the US$ 150 million needed to interrupt transmission and US$ 380 million for certification and integration in 2004–2005. It recalls the 2003 funding shortfalls that forced activities to be cancelled and describes resource mobilization efforts targeting G8 countries.

Discusses the need for a reliable supply of quality polio vaccines, including about 2.5 billion doses of WHO-prequalified OPV for supplementary campaigns in 2004–2005, continued OPV production capacity for stockpiles and growing demand for inactivated vaccine. It then covers conflict-affected countries and areas, where special arrangements will be needed for immunization, certification and staff security. It also introduces communication, advocacy and social mobilization needs in endemic areas and donor countries.

Calls for stronger social mobilization in the last endemic areas to engage communities and counter rumours that have undermined trust, with attention to vaccinator training, inclusion of women and suitable communication materials. It then covers biocontainment, setting deadlines for countries to inventory laboratories holding wild poliovirus by the end of 2004 and to destroy materials or move to higher containment levels later. It notes the particular challenge of containment in facilities producing inactivated vaccine from wild poliovirus.

Opens the chapter on the role of partners, describing governments of endemic, recently endemic and polio-free countries as owners and beneficiaries of the initiative who contribute cash and in-kind resources. It then outlines the roles of the spearheading partners, WHO, providing technical leadership, coordination and surveillance support, and Rotary International, which has committed over US$ 500 million and mobilized volunteers through its PolioPlus programme. It begins describing the contributions of UNICEF and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Describes the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's support, including funding for OPV, staff for surveillance and outbreak investigations and advanced virological expertise to trace virus origins. It covers international development agencies such as those of Germany, Canada, the United States, Japan and the United Kingdom, which had given or pledged US$ 1.76 billion, 59% of all funds for 1985–2005. It also notes that the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation is the largest donor after the Rotary Foundation, with US$ 75 million committed.

Describes a loan buy-down mechanism set up by the World Bank with foundations and Rotary to purchase polio vaccine for Nigeria and Pakistan, concessional loans from development banks, and private-sector fundraising. It covers international humanitarian organizations, with Red Cross and Red Crescent societies supporting campaigns and volunteer mobilization and the ICRC facilitating access to conflict zones. It notes that NGOs such as the Albert B. Sabin Vaccine Institute, Médecins sans Frontières and Save the Children support advocacy and have reached children in conflict-affected countries.

Describes the role of vaccine manufacturers in supplying enough quality-controlled polio vaccine on time, working with UNICEF and WHO on demand forecasts and production planning, and conducting research on products needed after certification.

Opens the chapter on 2009 and beyond, the phase of stopping OPV worldwide, explaining that both long-term and time-limited activities will be needed after certification, though costs cannot yet be estimated. It describes long-term needs such as independent verification of poliovirus containment and management of monovalent OPV stockpiles. It outlines time-limited measures against vaccine-derived poliovirus, such as maintaining acute flaccid paralysis surveillance for at least two years after OPV cessation and possibly environmental sampling or pre-cessation campaigns.

Notes that partners supplying routine vaccines, such as GAVI, will be central to decisions on post-OPV vaccination, and that financial needs will depend on international decisions in 2005–2007 about OPV cessation, stockpiles and other polio vaccines.
The back cover listing WHO as a spearheading partner of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative, with its Geneva address and contact details.
